chunks: From him, from Moalla, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Washa, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), and Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahboub, from Abu Wallad al-Hannat, and Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

It is from the correctness of the conviction of the Muslim man that he does not please the people by angering Allah, and he does not blame them for what Allah did not give him, for sustenance is not brought by the greed of the greedy, nor is it repelled by the dislike of the disliking; and if one of you were to flee from his sustenance as he flees from death, his sustenance would overtake him just as death overtakes him. Then he said: Indeed, Allah, by His justice and fairness, made relief and comfort to be in conviction and contentment, and made worry and grief to be in doubt and anger.
ai.seo_question: What are the signs of correct conviction (yaqin) in a Muslim according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: In al-Kafi, this hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) defines the practical manifestation of *yaqin* (certainty) as maintaining divine pleasure over human approval, a core tenet of Shia ethical theology. It underscores that *rizq* (sustenance) is divinely decreed and inevitable, thereby linking spiritual tranquility to acceptance of God's will and identifying anxiety as a symptom of doubt (*shakk*). This narrative serves as a foundational text for understanding the psychological and spiritual dimensions of trust in God (*tawakkul*) within the Shia tradition.
